content.overview: General defences defeat or reduce liability when the claimant otherwise establishes a prima facie tort. Core defences include volenti non fit injuria, plaintiff's default, act of God, private defence, necessity, statutory authority, and (in limited settings) inevitable accident.

sections.heading: Volenti non fit injuria
sections.body: A person who freely and knowingly consents to a risk cannot complain of harm within that risk (Smith v. Baker line of authority as received). Consent must be free, informed as to nature and extent of risk, and not vitiated by coercion or statute. Rescue cases and unequal bargaining often defeat a crude volenti plea.

sections.heading: Other defences
sections.body: Plaintiff's own fault may reduce or bar recovery depending on the tort and statute. Act of God requires an extraordinary natural event not reasonably foreseeable. Statutory authority protects acts compelled or authorised by statute if carried out without negligence beyond the authority. Private defence and necessity are narrowly applied.

sections.heading: Track B
sections.body: Plead defences specifically. Lead evidence of knowledge, consent, or statutory mandate. Do not confuse volenti with mere awareness of danger at work without free agreement.

enhancement.definition: General defences in tort are recognised circumstances in which a defendant avoids or limits liability even though a claimant alleges a tort.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Liability is qualified by consent, necessity, lawful authority, unavoidable events and the claimant's own conduct, depending on the tort.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Indian tort law is largely uncodified. The governing rules are developed through common-law principles, Indian judicial decisions and applicable legislation for particular fields; no statute should be treated as a general codification of this topic.
essentialIngredients: Prove every condition of that defence

Confirmed para 22: definition and ingredients of Act of God (vis major) as an extraordinary, violent, and irresistible operation of natural forces unconnected with human agency that could not be reasonably anticipated or resisted by human care and skill.

Confirmed paras 22–26: relationship between Act of God and negligence; natural forces do not absolve liability where antecedent or concurrent negligence is established (citing Greenock Corporation and S. Vedantacharya, 1987).
Confirmed para 26: onus of proving inevitable accident and general defences lies squarely on the defendant.

Common-law and statutory framework check: General defences in Indian tort law (volenti non fit injuria, inevitable accident, act of God, statutory authority, private defence, necessity) operate under uncodified common law received under Article 372 and pleadable in civil defense under the CPC.

distinctions.title: Volenti is based on informed consent to risk; contributory negligence concerns the claimant's failure to take reasonable care and generally affects damages.
distinctions.left: Volenti non fit injuria: complete defense barring claim; requires free consent and knowledge of full risk (sciens et volens).
distinctions.right: Contributory negligence: partial defense reducing quantum; requires failure by claimant to take reasonable care for own safety.

rows.left: Voluntary agreement to run the specific legal risk
rows.right: Carelessness or failure to exercise ordinary care

distinctions.title: Inevitable accident concerns an event not preventable by reasonable care; Act of God is confined to extraordinary natural forces.
distinctions.left: Inevitable accident: physically unavoidable accident despite exercise of ordinary caution and skill; may involve human or mechanical agency.
distinctions.right: Act of God (vis major): direct, violent and irresistible operation of elementary natural forces unconnected with human agency.

rows.left: May arise from human conduct, mechanical failure or agency
rows.right: Exclusively elementary natural forces without human intervention

rows.left: Not preventable by ordinary care, caution and skill
rows.right: Extraordinary natural event that could not be reasonably anticipated

caseLaw.name: Vohra Sadikbhai Rajakbhai v. State of Gujarat
caseLaw.holding: Judgment dated 10/05/2016. The Supreme Court comprehensively expounded the general defence of Act of God (vis major) in tort law, defining it as an extraordinary, direct, violent and irresistible act of nature which could not reasonably be anticipated or resisted by human skill. The Court held that the defence does not absolve the defendant from tort liability where antecedent or concurrent negligence exists (such as failing to maintain safe water levels in a dam prior to monsoon rains). The burden of proving an inevitable accident or Act of God rests strictly on the defendant.
caseLaw.relevance: Direct authoritative Supreme Court exposition on the ingredients, limits, and burden of proof for the general defence of Act of God (vis major) and inevitable accident in Indian tort law.
